frtb_sa_residual_risk_addon.text:
`frtb_ima_stressed_period_finder` answers "which stretch of history was the most stressful?" It slides a window across your full `returns` history, ranks each window by its Expected Shortfall at the chosen `confidence_level`, and returns the start index of the worst one. That window is what FRTB uses to calibrate the stressed ES in the internal models approach.

`frtb_sa_residual_risk_addon` answers a different question: "how much extra capital is needed for risks the standard approach's sensitivities-based method doesn't capture?" It takes `notionals` and `rrao_weights` per instrument and sums notional times weight, with no return history involved.

So one is a historical, return-based search for a window in the internal models approach. The other is a notional-based add-on in the standardised approach.

explain.text: `frtb_ima_stressed_period_finder` (FRTB IMA Stressed Period Finder) locates the stressed period used to calibrate stressed Expected Shortfall under FRTB's internal models approach. It slides a fixed-length window across your full return history, measures the Expected Shortfall of each window as a tail mean, and returns the start index of the window where that figure is largest. You supply `returns`, and can optionally set `window` (default 250 trading days) and `confidence_level` (default 0.975) used to rank the windows. pyvar does the calculation, so you get the start index of the worst window in your data.

when.text:
Use the FRTB IMA Stressed Period Finder (`frtb_ima_stressed_period_finder`) when you need to know which stretch of history was the most stressful for a portfolio:

- You have a full return history (`returns`) and want the start index of the 250-day window whose Expected Shortfall is largest, so the stressed ES can be calibrated to it.
- You want windows ranked by tail loss at a chosen `confidence_level`, which defaults to 0.975.
- You want a window length other than the FRTB standard of 250 trading days; you can change `window`.
- For the regulatory ES at 97.5%, look at `frtb_ima_expected_shortfall`, listed as the FRTB IMA Expected Shortfall.
